source.title: Improved Techniques for Optimization-Based Jailbreaking on Large Language Models
source.authors: Xiao-Jun Jia; Tianyu Pang; Chao Du; Yi-Hao Huang; Jindong Gu; Yang Liu; Xiao-Chun Cao; Min Lin

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendix are present. Some figure text is OCR-garbled, but the relevant tabular results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether optimized adversarial suffixes elicit harmful compliance, using GCG and an improved suffix-optimization attack. It tests the suffix-attack part of V4, not the other listed bypass mechanisms.
record.gate_note: The paper reports attack success rates for optimized suffix attacks and their variants. It does not report fine-tuning, aligned-versus-base per-token KL, compliant-prefix, or decoding-change experiments. Results from cited work and comparator methods not needed to capture suffix-attack outcomes are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports attack success rates of optimized adversarial suffixes (GCG, I-GCG) against chat models on AdvBench, HarmBench and in transfer. This bears on V4's claim that suffixes defeat refusal. It also argues that forcing a compliant opening ('Sure, here is') alone often fails because the model recovers and refuses. It is an attack-method paper, so many rows compare its own method with GCG/MAC; the ASRs still measure harmful compliance under suffix attack.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that harmful-guidance targets, automatic multi-coordinate updating and easy-to-hard initialization improve GCG, and that I-GCG reaches about 100% ASR on four 7B models and on the NeurIPS 2023 Red Teaming Track. They also find harmful guidance mainly drives effectiveness, while the other two techniques mainly drive efficiency. They note that transferability remains limited.
record.recipe_differences: This is an optimization-based adversarial-suffix attack study, not fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples or training to distribute safety across response positions. It adapts GCG with harmful target guidance, multi-coordinate updates, and suffix initialization.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies by model and by whether a suffix is evaluated on the model used to generate it or transferred to another target. On LLAMA2-7B-CHAT, GCG reports 54% while I-GCG reports 100%; reported transfer rates are much lower than the on-model rates.
record.problems: The study reports no uncertainty estimates. The NeurIPS Red Teaming Track result does not name the evaluated model in its table. The transfer results show low rates on several targets; the paper does not report a compliant-prefix or decoding-change experiment.
record.rows_left_out: Comparator attack results in Table 1 and competition baselines in Table 2 were not extracted because they are not needed to record the study's GCG/I-GCG suffix-attack outcomes. Average iteration counts and loss curves were left out because they measure optimization efficiency rather than harmful compliance.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant start and decoding changes are not tested; only optimized suffixes are.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models is not measured.
Parameter localization of safety is not studied.
Causes of shallowness are not studied.

missing.what: Qualitative finding that GCG suffixes make the model output the target opening ('Sure, here is...') but it then refuses. The authors argue opening-only targets are insufficient to jailbreak. No rate is given for how often the opening was matched but refusal followed.

record.verdict_notes: ASR is judged by a refusal-string check, then a GPT-3.5 classifier, then manual review, on only 50 AdvBench requests. No uncertainty is reported. Most rows compare the study's own method with GCG/MAC, but they still report harmful-compliance rates under suffix attack. The paper's observation that matching the compliant opening does not guarantee harmful continuation is the result most relevant to the shallow-alignment mechanism, and it is only qualitative.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples and its effect on harmful compliance.
Fine-tuning on benign data and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
The study tests optimized suffix attacks. It does not test compliant prefilling or decoding changes.
Whether safety behaviour is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
Training safety beyond initial response tokens and testing its robustness.

relationships.condition: On-model suffix attacks on AdvBench against LLAMA2-7B-CHAT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT-0.2, plus weakly aligned Vicuna/Guanaco
relationships.reason: I-GCG reaches 100% on all four models, including Llama2-7B-chat (up from 54% with GCG), and GCG reaches 92–98% on Mistral, Vicuna and Guanaco (r1–r4, r6–r8, r26–r31).
relationships.display_finding: I-GCG reached 100% on all four models, including Llama2-7B-chat where GCG reached 54%, and GCG reached 92–98% on Mistral, Vicuna and Guanaco.

relationships.condition: A plain 'Sure, here is' suffix target on LLAMA2-7B-CHAT, and suffixes transferred from Vicuna to other models
relationships.reason: GCG gets only 54% on Llama2-7B-chat (r5, r22). Adding harmful self-suggestion to the target raises this to 82% (r23). The text says models refuse even after matching the 'Sure' opening. Transferred suffixes reach 0–26% (r10–r21).
relationships.display_finding: GCG with the plain target reached 54% on Llama2-7B-chat, and adding harmful self-suggestion to the target raised this to 82%. Models could still refuse after producing the 'Sure' opening, and transferred suffixes reached only 0–26%.
